bilingual.en: For many pregnant women, understanding what seafood is safe and healthy and what should be avoided because of mercury concerns comes with a lot of worrying. In part, that's because the federal government's advice on the matter, first issued in 2004, has long been criticized as vague. That guidance has included advice on how much seafood to eat, and which species pregnant and breastfeeding women should avoid over concerns about mercury contamination. But critics say the government advisory has done more harm than good, scaring many pregnant and breastfeeding women away from eating seafood altogether.
bilingual.zh: 对许多孕妇来说，了解哪些海产品安全且有益健康，以及哪些海产品因担心汞而应当避免，会带来许多忧虑。部分原因在于，联邦政府首次于2004年发布的相关建议长期以来一直被批评含糊不清。该指导意见包括关于应食用多少海产品，以及孕妇和哺乳期女性因担心汞污染而应避免哪些种类的建议。但批评者表示，政府的这份指导意见弊大于利，使许多孕妇和哺乳期女性彻底不敢食用海产品。

bilingual.en: The problem is real. According to a spokesman for the Food and Drug Administration, or FDA for short, the agency analyzed fish consumption data from more than 1,000 pregnant women in the US and found that 21 per cent of them ate no fish whatsoever in the previous month. And those who did eat fish consumed far less than recommended by the dietary guidelines. Some 50 per cent ate less than two ounces a week and 75 per cent ate less than four ounces.
bilingual.zh: 这个问题确实存在。据美国食品药品监督管理局（简称FDA）一位发言人介绍，该机构分析了美国一千多名孕妇的鱼类食用数据，发现其中21%在前一个月完全没有吃鱼。而那些吃鱼的人，摄入量也远低于膳食指南的建议。约50%的人每周摄入量少于两盎司，75%的人少于四盎司。

bilingual.en: This week the FDA issued an update to the advice, listing more than sixty species in a chart that ranks fish as A Best Choice, Good Choice and Choices to Avoid. The goal is to make it easier for mothers-to-be to feel confident about the type of seafood they include in their diets. The new advice recommends consumers choose a variety of fish to eat, and it comes with an easy-to-understand illustration of what an appropriate portion size should be—four ounces for an adult and two ounces for children aged four to seven.
bilingual.zh: 本周，FDA更新了相关建议，在一张图表中列出六十多种鱼类，并将其分为“最佳选择”“不错的选择”和“应避免的选择”。此举旨在让准妈妈更容易对自己饮食中所摄入的海产品种类感到放心。新建议推荐消费者食用多种鱼类，并配有一幅易于理解的图示，说明适当的食用分量应为多少：成年人四盎司，四至七岁的儿童两盎司。

text: I know you're busy with work, but you also need to take some time off to recharge those batteries. So, should you plan one big vacation for the year, or should you take multiple short vacations throughout? Quantity can sometimes beat quality. First and foremost, regardless of how you use your vacation days, you need to be using them, and soon. The longer you put off your time off, the worse you're making things for yourself. One 9-year-long study published in Psychosomatic Medicine suggests not taking at least one vacation a year may increase your risk of mortality due to heart disease. So, not only are you killing your joy, you're possibly killing yourself. Give yourself a break, folks. When you should take those breaks, however, depends on a few factors: how many days you have available to use, what activities bring you joy, whether you have a family or not, and other variables come into play. Because of that, there's no perfect formula that works for everyone, but there are still a few things everyone can try to shoot for. We know that in terms of maximizing relaxation, you should aim for vacations that range somewhere between 7 and 11 days long. That gives you enough time to let go of your stress at work, completely loosen up, and achieve full-on calm. That above-mentioned study also recommends you space out your vacations evenly instead of using up all of your days at once. Eight days might sound like a lot for someone who only gets 10 days of vacation a year. But if you frame them with weekends, you can manage two evenly spaced 8-day vacations a year. If you have 14 days of paid leave, that's almost three separate 8-day vacations you can use to split your year into thirds. As tempting as it might be to use all your days to take one long summer break, your overall goal should be to achieve the perfect balance between length plus joy and frequency. Vacation frequency is important because planning multiple breaks throughout the year means you always have something to look forward to. Planning things and the anticipation that comes with it tend to make us happier. If you only take one long vacation every year, the excitement builds much more slowly and seems so far off that it can actually lead to feelings of despair.

text: Autonomous cars that can take over from drivers if they are tired or caught in the heat of an argument are being developed in Sweden. Researchers working as part of the European Union's €77 billion research program are developing sensor-based systems that monitor whether a driver is distracted, anxious or tired. If a driver is not in a fit state to be on the road, the car automatically takes control of the wheel to prevent accidents. Doctor Anna Anund from the Swedish National Road and Transport Research Institute, who is leading the project, said a driver's state can be measured using a number of sensors, including heart rate monitors and eye sensors, which track where a driver's gaze is. She said the aim was to really make sure that the transition from the driver to the vehicle is done in a safe way, so we can take into consideration the driver's state, and so we do not give control to a driver who is under pressure of fatigue, stress, anxiety, and so on. According to data from the European Commission, Sweden has the safest roads in the EU, with the UK a close second. However, the number of road accidents in both has largely levelled out since 2010. Driver fatigue is thought to be responsible for as many as a fifth of road crashes across the EU, although there are certain times of the day when more accidents happen. At 6:00 a.m., for example, drivers are said to be 20 times more likely to have an accident than at 10:00 a.m. While most experts agree driverless technology should help bring down accident numbers in the long term, some have questioned whether it is safe. The researchers have said the technology they are developing is seeking to bridge the gap between Level 3 on the autonomy scale, in which drivers have to be ready to take control of the car at any point, and Level 4, in which driving is automated. Daniel Ruiz, the chief executive of the UK's connected and autonomous vehicle programme Meridian, said: "there is a strong debate going on about how it is possible to make a Level 3 car completely safe." Despite advances in technology, we still have some way to go in shifting public sentiment. With an increase in attention-grabbing accidents recently, drivers now view self-driving cars as less safe than they used to.

text: W: Hi, Frank, are you working through your lunch hour again? M: No, not at all. It's my 10th wedding anniversary next week, and I promised Jane that I would book a city break for us, as I have annual leave to take, and it would be nice to celebrate somewhere warm. So, I'm trying to book something in Barcelona. W: That sounds so romantic. I adore Barcelona. It's such a fabulous cosmopolitan city. There's so much to do there, excellent food, and that cathedral that they are still building after about 150 years. Very cool. M: I know. But the anniversary is looming, and I'm still scrambling to find accommodation. Everything is either wildly expensive or already fully booked. I'm starting to feel a bit frantic. W: Well, if you are going for a whole week, why don't you do a couple of nights in somewhere really glamorous, and then do the rest of the week a bit further up the coast, where the accommodation is cheaper, and that will offset the cost of the expensive place? M: That might be a good plan. It's not too expensive to rent a car, so we could still drive into the city. Yes, there are lots of places outside the city that have pools and are all inclusive, so we wouldn't even need to pay for food or drinks. I'll send a query now about the dates we're interested in. W: That sounds perfect. I'm sure that Jane will be absolutely thrilled to bits. I really do recommend visiting that cathedral. You can go all the way up to the top of it, but you need to go up a really steep spiral staircase to get there. M: Considering Jane is terrified of heights, I think if I tried to make her do that, I would come back divorced. Thanks for the help though; it was turning into a logistical nightmare.

text: W: Hey there, Paul. How's it going? M: Hi, Suzanne. Just keeping busy with the usual stuff, filling prescriptions, talking to patients about their medications, that kind of thing. How about you? W: Same here, although I did have an interesting case come in this morning. A patient came in, inquiring about a medication that had a potential interaction with another medication she was already taking. M: Oh, that's always tricky. What did you do? W: I explained the issue to her as best I could, and recommended she double-check with her doctor. And you know what? She actually followed my advice, and the doctor ended up switching the patient's medication. M: Ah, that's great. You must feel quite accomplished. W: Totally. These moments are the highlights of my routine work, employing my pharmaceutical expertise to the benefit of people's health and well-being. M: I fully agree. Unfortunately, the opposite is true when the patient is too stubborn and they refuse to listen to us. W: So true. In other developments, we've had a lot of people coming in to get their flu shots, which is always good to see. M: Good, good. I've been working on a new medication therapy management program for our patients with chronic conditions. It helps patients manage their medications more effectively. W: That sounds interesting. M: We review all of their medications, and make sure that they're taking them as prescribed. We also look for any potential drug interactions or side effects. Patient response has so far been very positive. Some have reported seeing improvements in their health, which is really rewarding to see. W: That's great to hear. Do you use text message reminders? M: Yes, absolutely. W: It's a great idea. Medication non-adherence is a big problem, especially for older patients. M: We're still in the early stages of the program, but I'm hopeful that it will make a real difference for our patients.

text: In America, at least, passion is a word that often comes up on job descriptions and in interviews. On the whole, passionate people are thought of in a positive light and considered likely to achieve their goals. But when it comes to predicting achievement, has the importance of passion been overstated? According to a new study from Stanford University, passion may be less important in certain cultures, and the fact that passion is often seen as a key to achievement may reflect a distinctly Western model of motivation. The chief factor explored in the study was how individualistic a society was. In individualistic cultures, the researchers assert, people are more motivated by pursuing paths related to their passions, but those in collectivistic cultures are more likely to see themselves as part of a network. They often place fulfilling obligations to others above focusing on their own interests. The researchers looked at data from nearly 60 countries. They found that in science subjects, passion was positively correlated with academic achievements. Higher levels of enjoyment and interest also bolstered test scores. But the strength of this correlation wasn't the same across cultures. Those in individualistic societies such as the U.S., Australia, and the UK showed a stronger link between passion and achievement. The effect of passion on performance was more subtle for those in more collectivistic societies such as Colombia or Thailand. These findings were mirrored in achievement in both mathematics and reading. It's clear from the findings that passion isn't the only thing that motivates people to achieve their goals.

text: Why does nature create patterns? The reason patterns often appear in nature is simple: the same basic physical or chemical processes occur in many pattern substances and organisms as they form. Whether in plants and animals or rocks, foams and ice crystals, the intricate patterns that happen in nature come down to what's happening at the level of atoms and molecules. A pattern in nature is any regularly repeated arrangement of shapes or colors. Some of the most striking examples include the six-sided arrays of rocks at Giant's Causeway in the United Kingdom, and the colorful stripes and spots on tropical fish. Patterns like these begin to form at a small scale when materials undergo processes like drying, freezing, wrinkling, diffusing and reacting. Those changes then give rise to complex patterns at a larger scale that people can see. Imagine delicate frozen crystals on a window during winter. What creates that pattern? When water freezes, its molecules begin clustering together. Water molecules have a particular bent shape that causes them to stack into clusters as they freeze. As the cluster grows, many outside factors, including humidity and temperature, begin to affect its overall shape. If the water is freezing on a window, for example, random imperfections on the glass surface affect the stacking and create the larger pattern. But scientists do not always know the purpose of a pattern, or even if there is one. The molecular processes involved are simple enough that they might generate a pattern by coincidence.

text: Many people, myself included, have multiple areas of life they would like to improve. For example, I would like to reach more people with my writing, to lift heavier weights at the gym, and to start practising mindfulness more consistently. Those are just a few of the goals I find desirable, and you probably have a long list yourself. The problem is, even if we are committed to working hard on our goals, our natural tendency is to return to our old habits at some point. Making a permanent lifestyle change is really difficult. Recently I've come across a few studies that will make these difficult lifestyle changes a bit easier. As you'll see, however, the approach to mastering many areas of life is somewhat counterintuitive. Research has shown that you are two to three times more likely to stick with your habits if you make a specific plan for when, where, and how you will perform the behavior. For example, in one study, scientists asked people to fill out a sentence to specify during the next week they would do at least 20 minutes of vigorous exercise on which day, at what time of day, and at or in what place. Researchers found that people who filled out this sentence were two to three times more likely to actually exercise compared to a control group who did not make plans for their future behavior. Psychologists call these specific plans implementation intentions because they state when, where, and how you intend to implement a particular behavior. However, follow-up research has discovered implementation intentions only work when you focus on one thing at a time. In fact, researchers found that people who tried to accomplish multiple goals were less committed and less likely to succeed than those who focused on a single goal. Another science-based reason to focus on one thing at a time is that when you begin practising a new habit, it requires a lot of conscious effort to remember to do it. After a while, however, the pattern of behavior becomes easier. Eventually, your new habit becomes a normal routine, and the process is more or less mindless and automatic. The most important thing to note is that there is some tipping point at which new habits become more or less automatic. The time it takes to build a habit depends on many factors, including how difficult the habit is, your genetics, and more.

bilingual.en: Many people, myself included, have multiple areas of life they would like to improve. For example, I would like to reach more people with my writing, to lift heavier weights at the gym, and to start practising mindfulness more consistently. Those are just a few of the goals I find desirable, and you probably have a long list yourself. The problem is, even if we are committed to working hard on our goals, our natural tendency is to return to our old habits at some point. Making a permanent lifestyle change is really difficult.
bilingual.zh: 包括我在内，许多人都希望改善生活中的多个方面。例如，我希望通过写作让更多人读到我的作品，希望在健身房举起更重的重量，也希望开始更加持续地练习正念。这些只是我认为值得追求的几个目标，而你自己可能也列有一长串目标。问题在于，即使我们决心为目标努力奋斗，我们的自然倾向仍然是在某个时候回到旧有习惯。要永久改变生活方式确实非常困难。

bilingual.en: Recently I've come across a few studies that will make these difficult lifestyle changes a bit easier. As you'll see, however, the approach to mastering many areas of life is somewhat counterintuitive. Research has shown that you are two to three times more likely to stick with your habits if you make a specific plan for when, where, and how you will perform the behavior. For example, in one study, scientists asked people to fill out a sentence to specify during the next week they would do at least 20 minutes of vigorous exercise on which day, at what time of day, and at or in what place. Researchers found that people who filled out this sentence were two to three times more likely to actually exercise compared to a control group who did not make plans for their future behavior. Psychologists call these specific plans implementation intentions because they state when, where, and how you intend to implement a particular behavior.
bilingual.zh: 最近，我接触到了一些研究，这些研究将使这些艰难的生活方式改变变得稍微容易一些。不过，正如你将看到的，掌握生活中许多方面的方法有些违背直觉。研究表明，如果你针对自己将在何时、何地以及如何实施某种行为制订具体计划，那么坚持这些习惯的可能性会提高到原来的两到三倍。例如，在一项研究中，科学家要求人们填写一个句子，具体说明自己将在下一周的哪一天、一天中的什么时间，以及在什么地点进行至少20分钟的剧烈运动。研究人员发现，与没有为未来行为制订计划的对照组相比，填写了这个句子的人实际进行锻炼的可能性高出两到三倍。心理学家将这些具体计划称为“执行意图”，因为它们说明了你打算在何时、何地以及如何实施某种特定行为。

bilingual.en: Another science-based reason to focus on one thing at a time is that when you begin practising a new habit, it requires a lot of conscious effort to remember to do it. After a while, however, the pattern of behavior becomes easier. Eventually, your new habit becomes a normal routine, and the process is more or less mindless and automatic. The most important thing to note is that there is some tipping point at which new habits become more or less automatic. The time it takes to build a habit depends on many factors, including how difficult the habit is, your genetics, and more.
bilingual.zh: 一次专注于一件事还有一个基于科学的理由，那就是当你开始练习一种新习惯时，记得去做这件事需要付出大量有意识的努力。然而，过一段时间之后，这种行为模式会变得更加容易。最终，你的新习惯会成为一种日常惯例，而这一过程或多或少会变得无需意识参与，并且自动进行。需要注意的最重要一点是，存在这样一个临界点：在此之后，新习惯会或多或少地变得自动化。养成一个习惯所需的时间取决于许多因素，包括习惯的难度、你的遗传因素，以及其他因素。

text: It was a lazy, hazy, crazy day on the dwarf planet Pluto when New Horizons, a spacecraft from Earth, flew by at a speed of 31,000 mph (miles per hour) two years ago. The spacecraft took a bunch of photos, made some quick measurements of Pluto's atmosphere, and sent them all back here, giving planetary scientists their first up-close look of the distant dwarf planet. One of the more bizarre things they found was that the haze in Pluto's atmosphere was much thicker than previously thought. The planet also had an atmosphere much cooler than earlier estimates, topping out at −333.4°F. Now, a study published in Nature links those two atmospheric observations. A computer model developed by planetary scientist Xi Zhang and colleagues shows the haze of tiny droplets in the upper atmosphere is likely scattering light from the Sun, preventing heat from reaching the planet below. We see hazy skies on Earth too, from time to time, whenever solid particles get suspended in the air—from water-based fogs, to ash from fires, to the toxic droplets that make up a thick smog. But on Earth, the overall temperature of the planet is dominated by the distribution of gases in our atmosphere. On Pluto, the authors suggest, haze might be more influential. Particles can reflect light from the Sun here on Earth: It happens after volcanoes erupt, emitting clouds of particles that reflect the Sun's rays into the atmosphere. Some people even propose imitating this phenomenon to alleviate the effects of climate change. But our planet isn't dominated by that process, or at least it hasn't been for a few billion years. If Pluto's atmosphere is very different from ours and from that of other nearby planets, it could help scientists expand their understanding of planetary atmospheres. But right now, this is just a good guess based on data from New Horizons and a sophisticated computer model, not direct observations of the haze's composition. There are other theories floating around to explain Pluto's cool temperatures, including blaming the cold air on gases in the atmosphere. Luckily, the authors will get a chance to test their notions when the James Webb Space Telescope launches later. That observatory can detect different spectrums of light, which the hazy Plutonian atmosphere would be positively glowing with as it scattered sunlight. The researchers just have to wait and see if the light from the telescope validates their bright idea.

text: Parents have a small window where they can influence their 8- to 10-year-old children's music taste, researchers have concluded. The 24-month time frame comes at an age when youngsters are old enough to appreciate poetic lyrics and snappy tunes, but have not yet started to be embarrassed by their mother and father's preferences. Dr. Hauke Egermann, a lecturer in music at the University of York, carried out a literature review into more than a dozen studies looking at parental musical influence. "Children have an openness to new music, and this means parents have an important role to play in developing the musical preferences of their kids," he said. However, time is of the essence as parental influence is most likely to be effective during the critical time period before age ten. During adolescence, children tend to gravitate away from their parents' choices and are more influenced by their peers. A separate survey of 2,000 British parents by music streaming service Deezer also found that nearly four-fifths of parents agreed that their children were far more receptive to their musical suggestions before the age of ten. In contrast, just 10 percent of parents reported positive reactions from their teenage children when they shared their favorite music. Some 79 percent of fathers said they had tried to influence their children's music, but just 69 percent of mothers. However, mothers were more effective, with 38 percent reporting that their kids loved the tunes they shared, compared to 30 percent of dads who, in some cases, said their children cried or even fell asleep. Dr. Egermann claims introducing children to a variety of musical styles is the key to fostering good taste in later life. "By playing children a variety of genres before this critical period, research on familiarization suggests they will enjoy lots of different types of music as adults," he added. The benefits of having a wider taste in music include the ability to manage their emotions more effectively, socialize and bond with others more easily, and to have a better understanding of other cultures as well. Dr. Egermann advises parents not to push their favorite music too hard on their children, but instead play it as background music while a child is playing. They can also help create positive memories about artists and bands by going to concerts and live music events together.

text: The line chart illustrates the changes in the gross enrolment ratio in higher education in China from 1990 to 2019. As is clearly shown, the figure witnessed a steady and remarkable upward trend over these three decades. In 1990, only 3.4% of the eligible population entered higher education. In my view, such progress not only improves individual prospects but also strengthens the nation's competitiveness. In conclusion, the steady climb of the enrolment ratio speaks volumes about how far Chinese higher education has advanced, and I firmly believe this positive momentum will continue in the years ahead.

text: It has become a common phenomenon that young people spend a great deal of time online, yet many of them struggle to tell trustworthy information from falsehood. As the passage notes, they are often unable to recognize false information, judge the reliability of online sources, or distinguish real news from fake stories. This deficiency in digital judgment, though easily overlooked, deserves our serious attention. The consequences are far from trivial. Misled by fabricated news, young people may form distorted views of the world, make ill-informed decisions, and even spread rumours unknowingly. Since their critical-thinking skills are still developing, they are especially vulnerable to eye-catching yet groundless claims that circulate rapidly across social media. To address this issue, concerted efforts are needed. First and foremost, schools should offer media-literacy courses that teach students how to verify facts and trace information back to its source. Meanwhile, online platforms ought to strengthen fact-checking and clearly label questionable content. Finally, young people themselves should cultivate the habit of cross-checking a story against several reliable sources before believing or sharing it. Only in this way can they navigate the digital world wisely.

text: The passage vividly presents a common scene: many teenagers today are obsessed with pop stars, copying how their idols talk and dress and spending heavily just to see them face to face. In my view, this phenomenon deserves a balanced judgement rather than blind praise or total denial. Admittedly, taking an admirable star as one's idol can be positively motivating, since a hard-working singer may inspire young people to pursue their own dreams. However, when admiration turns into blind worship, the harm outweighs the benefit. Chasing stars at great expense drains teenagers' limited money and time, distracts them from their studies, and may even distort their values. To address the issue, joint efforts are needed. Parents and schools should guide adolescents to build a rational view of idols, while the media ought to promote genuine role models instead of empty fame. For teenagers themselves, the key is to learn from a star's strengths without losing themselves. Only in this way can idol worship become a source of growth rather than regret.

text: It is not uncommon nowadays that some parents in China are overprotective of their children. They arrange everything, make every decision on their behalf, and forbid any independent exploration for fear of mistakes or injuries. In my view, however well-intentioned this practice may be, it does far more harm than good. To begin with, such excessive protection deprives children of the chance to develop independence. When every choice is made for them, they never learn how to weigh options or solve problems on their own. Moreover, being shielded from all failure leaves them without resilience; a child who has never fallen simply does not know how to stand up again. As a result, these children may grow into adults who are competent in theory yet helpless in real life. To address this issue, parents should first loosen their grip and let children make age-appropriate decisions by themselves. In addition, they ought to treat mistakes as valuable lessons rather than disasters to be avoided at all costs. Ultimately, the wisest parents shift their role from controllers to guides, offering support from behind instead of clearing every obstacle ahead.

text: Nowadays more and more people choose to live an environmentally friendly lifestyle. This shift is no longer a slogan but a set of daily habits that reshape how we eat, travel and consume. Several concrete practices explain this trend. To begin with, many commuters now favour buses, subways or shared bikes over private cars, which cuts carbon emission and eases traffic. What is more, sorting rubbish into recyclable and kitchen waste has become routine in my own neighbourhood, so that plastic and paper can be recycled rather than buried. Take myself as an example: since I started carrying a cloth bag and a reusable bottle, I have thrown away far less single-use plastic every week. Small as these acts seem, they add up to a sustainable way of living. As a result, an environmentally friendly lifestyle benefits both individuals and the planet. It saves resources, keeps the air cleaner and reminds us that a green future depends on the choices we make today. I firmly believe that when everyone takes one small step, the earth will thank us tomorrow.

text: Nowadays more and more people keep learning new skills to adapt to a fast-changing world. This trend, in my view, is not a passing fashion but a wise and even necessary response to the age we live in. The most obvious reason lies in the speed of technological change. Skills that guaranteed a stable job ten years ago may become outdated overnight, so those who stop learning risk being replaced. Take my cousin as an example. As a traditional accountant, she felt threatened when her company introduced financial software, yet instead of complaining she spent her evenings mastering data analysis. Within a year she was promoted rather than laid off. Her experience convinces me that continuous learning is what keeps a person competitive. Beyond the workplace, learning also enriches our daily life and broadens our horizons. In conclusion, keeping pace with a changing world through lifelong learning is no longer optional but essential. Rather than fearing change, we should treat every new skill as a bridge to a wider future. I firmly believe that whoever embraces new skills today will stand firm tomorrow.

text: Nowadays more and more people take delight in offering help to the needy. This heart-warming trend, in my view, reflects both a growing sense of social responsibility and the genuine happiness that giving brings to the giver. There are solid reasons behind this phenomenon. On the one hand, lending a hand to those in difficulty strengthens the bonds that hold a community together, and a single act of kindness often inspires others to follow. On the other hand, helping people is deeply rewarding in itself. I still remember one winter when my classmates and I spent a weekend teaching migrant children in a shabby rented room. We gained far more warmth from their bright smiles than we ever gave, and that experience convinced me that generosity enriches both sides. Therefore, we should never underestimate the power of a helping hand. If each of us is willing to reach out to those in need, our society will surely grow kinder, warmer and more united.

text: Nowadays more and more students are becoming increasingly aware of the importance of developing digital skills. This awareness is well founded, for in an age reshaped by technology, the ability to handle digital tools has become as basic as reading and writing. There are solid reasons behind this trend. For one thing, digital competence directly boosts academic efficiency. In my own case, learning to use spreadsheets and reference software turned a painful week of manual data sorting into an afternoon's work. Moreover, such skills open doors in the job market. For instance, a classmate who taught herself basic programming stood out among hundreds of applicants and landed an internship at a tech firm. As a result, students who master these tools gain a clear edge both in study and in career. In conclusion, the growing attention to digital skills reflects a genuine need rather than a passing fashion. Students would be wise to invest time in mastering practical tools instead of waiting until graduation, so that they can thrive in a world that runs on technology.

text: Today more and more people begin to realize the pleasures and joys of real-world social interaction. After years of staring at glowing screens, many of us have discovered that a warm handshake, a shared laugh or a face-to-face chat brings a satisfaction that no online message can replace. My own experience convinces me of this. Last summer I put down my phone and joined a hiking club in my hometown. Instead of typing emojis, I talked, sweated and cooked with real people on the trail. When a stranger offered me water on a steep slope, I felt a genuine bond that no number of online 'likes' had ever given me. Those weekends left me happier and more energetic than a whole year of scrolling ever did. Therefore, real-world social interaction feeds a need that technology alone cannot satisfy. It reminds us that we are living beings who thrive on presence, eye contact and shared moments. Let us step out of the virtual world more often and reconnect with the people around us, for it is there that true joy quietly grows.

text: It is now widely accepted that mutual trust and openness is the key to promoting cooperation. When people or organizations are willing to share information honestly and believe in each other's good intentions, they can join hands far more effectively than those who hold everything back. The reason is simple: trust removes the fear that keeps partners guarding themselves, while openness lets them pool their strengths toward a common goal. A telling example is my own experience in a group research project last term. At first, two members kept their data private, worried that others might take the credit, and our progress almost stalled. Once we agreed to be transparent and openly admitted our doubts, ideas flowed freely, tasks were divided fairly, and we finished ahead of schedule. The same logic explains why companies that communicate frankly with their partners tend to build lasting alliances rather than short-lived deals. In short, without trust and openness, cooperation is built on sand. Only when we dare to be honest and give others our confidence can genuine collaboration take root and bear fruit.

text: With the application of information technology in education, college students can now learn in more diverse and efficient ways. Not long ago, learning was confined to a fixed classroom and a single textbook, but technology has broken these limits and reshaped how we acquire knowledge. On the one hand, learning has become far more diverse. Through massive open online courses, a student in a small town can now attend lectures delivered by professors at top universities, which was once unthinkable, and digital libraries offer millions of books and papers at the click of a button. On the other hand, learning is remarkably efficient. Thanks to AI-powered tutors, questions that once took days to solve can be answered in seconds, and search engines help us locate exactly the material we need. As a result, we save time and study with greater focus. In conclusion, information technology has enriched both the variety and the speed of learning. text: In an era of information explosion, it is vitally important to develop the ability to think critically and make rational choices. Every day we are flooded with news, advertisements and social-media posts, yet not all of them are trustworthy. Only those who can sift truth from falsehood are able to stay clear-headed. text: Today increasing importance is being attached to cultivating college students' team spirit. Both universities and future employers have realized that few achievements today are the work of a single hand, so this quality truly deserves our attention. There are convincing reasons behind this trend. First, almost every modern task, from a laboratory experiment to a business start-up, demands that people with different strengths pool their efforts; without cooperation, even talented individuals can accomplish little. Second, working in a team teaches students to communicate patiently, respect different opinions, and share responsibility, all of which are qualities that textbooks alone can never provide. A student who once relied only on personal effort, for instance, may finally learn to trust others after completing a group project together. For these reasons, team spirit should never be treated as something optional. Colleges ought to design more group tasks, and students themselves should step out of their comfort zones and embrace cooperation, because it is teamwork that turns scattered abilities into real strength.

text: People are now increasingly aware of the danger of 'appearance anxiety' or being obsessed with one's looks. This uneasiness rarely appears out of nowhere. Bombarded daily by filtered images and narrow aesthetic standards on social media, many young people measure themselves against unreachable models and feel that they never look good enough. The key is to shift attention from the mirror to inner value — our knowledge, kindness and abilities. That moment taught me that self-acceptance, rather than a flawless appearance, is what sets us free. In short, looks are only a thin surface of who we are. Once we learn to value character over appearance, 'appearance anxiety' loses its grip, and we can live with genuine confidence.

text: People are now increasingly aware of the challenges in making a decision when faced with too many choices. Ironically, the abundance of options that was meant to empower us often leaves us hesitant, anxious and exhausted instead. A personal experience makes this clear. Last semester, when I tried to pick an elective, the online system listed over sixty courses. I spent three whole evenings comparing descriptions, reading reviews and switching between tabs, yet I still felt uncertain and finally enrolled at random. The endless comparison drained my energy long before the real learning began, and it left me doubting whether I had chosen wisely at all. The lesson I have drawn is not to fear choices but to tame them. Before browsing, I now fix two or three criteria that truly matter to me and ignore the rest. By narrowing the field in advance, I turn an overwhelming list into a manageable shortlist, and I make decisions faster and with far less regret. When choices multiply, a clear standard, rather than more comparison, is what sets us free.

text: People are now increasingly aware of the 'digital gap' or challenges the elderly face in a digital world. As technology reshapes daily life at a dizzying speed, many senior citizens find themselves left behind, struggling to keep pace with tools that younger generations take for granted. This gap manifests itself in countless everyday scenes. For instance, an elderly man may stand helplessly before a restaurant that only accepts mobile payment, unable to scan the QR code. Similarly, when hospitals shift appointment booking online, or when a health code is required to enter public places, those unfamiliar with smartphones are effectively shut out. As a result, tasks that were once simple now become sources of anxiety and isolation. In my view, no one should be excluded by the very technology meant to serve them. Therefore, families ought to patiently teach their parents digital skills, while service providers should retain user-friendly alternatives such as cash counters and manual registration. Only through such joint efforts can we bridge this gap and build a society that is inclusive of every generation.

text: Today there is a growing awareness that mental well-being needs to be given as much attention as physical health. For too long, we have measured a person's health only by the body, ignoring the mind that quietly suffers behind a healthy-looking face. Yet a troubled mind can be just as disabling as a broken leg, which is why the two deserve equal care. My own experience convinces me of this. During my sophomore year, a close friend kept a perfect exercise routine but slid into deep anxiety before exams. He looked strong, so no one noticed until his grades and sleep collapsed. Only after he sought counseling did he truly recover. His story shows that neglecting the mind can undo all the benefits of a fit body. Therefore, we should treat mental and physical health as two wheels of the same cart. Schools and workplaces ought to offer counseling as readily as gyms, and each of us should learn to talk about our feelings without shame. When the mind is cared for as much as the body, a person can be genuinely, fully healthy.

text: When faced with differing opinions, we should try to reach agreement through friendly discussion and reasonable argument. In a world where people come from diverse backgrounds, disagreements are inevitable; yet how we handle them reveals our maturity. Rather than shouting others down or stubbornly clinging to our own views, seeking common ground through calm reasoning is always the wiser choice. The reason is simple: friendly discussion invites cooperation, while quarrels only deepen the divide. Take the famous debates in scientific communities. When Darwin proposed his theory of evolution, opponents raised sharp objections, but progress was made not by insults but by patient argument and shared evidence. Similarly, in my own study group, a heated dispute over a project was resolved only after we sat down, listened to one another, and combined our ideas. Mutual respect turned rivals into partners. In conclusion, differing opinions need not lead to conflict. If we approach them with an open mind, sound logic, and genuine respect, we can transform disagreement into understanding and reach a consensus that benefits everyone. This is not only a skill but a mark of a civilized society.

bilingual.en: It is widely accepted that an important goal of education is to help students learn how to learn. In my view, teaching learners to acquire knowledge on their own matters far more than simply filling their heads with facts, because the ability to learn lasts a lifetime. Consider two students: one memorizes every formula the teacher offers, and the other masters how to find, question and apply new information. For these reasons, education should do more than deliver content. Once students truly learn how to learn, they hold a key that opens every door throughout their lives.

text: As is known to all, gaining a sound knowledge of the basics is of vital importance for students to master an academic subject. It follows that students should never underestimate the value of the basics. Rather than rushing toward complicated tasks, we ought to devote patient effort to consolidating the fundamentals first. Only by standing on such firm ground can we climb steadily toward true mastery of any subject.

text: Nowadays parents are increasingly aware that allowing kids more freedom to explore and learn on their own helps foster their independence and boost their confidence. This shift in parenting reflects a valuable truth: children grow strongest not when every step is arranged for them, but when they are trusted to try, fail, and try again. To begin with, freedom teaches independence in a way no lecture ever could. A child who is allowed to plan a weekend trip, cook a simple meal, or solve a quarrel with friends gradually learns to rely on his own judgment. Take my younger cousin, for example. When his mother stopped correcting his every homework mistake and let him check the answers himself, his grades slowly improved, and, more importantly, he began tackling new problems without fear. Each small success became a brick building his confidence. In this way, granting children the room to explore freely is not a risk but a wise investment. As a result, they mature into adults who dare to think, decide, and stand on their own feet.

text: With their valuable skills and experience, elderly people can continue to make significant contributions to society. Far from being a burden, seniors possess a lifetime of professional knowledge and practical wisdom that younger generations simply have not had time to acquire. This potential shows itself in countless ways. Take retired engineers and doctors as an example: many of them return to their former posts as consultants, training newcomers and solving problems that puzzle less experienced staff. In my own community, retired teachers volunteer to run free evening classes, while elderly craftsmen pass down traditional skills that would otherwise disappear. Such efforts prove that age brings not decline but a rich resource waiting to be tapped. Therefore, we should stop regarding old age merely as a time of rest and instead recognize its true worth. If society creates more opportunities for the elderly to share their expertise, everyone benefits. Only by valuing and drawing on their skills and experience can we build a wiser and more harmonious community.

text: Nowadays more and more college students have come to realize social practice and academic learning are equally important. Only by letting them go hand in hand can college students grow into capable talents that society genuinely needs.

text: To increase the likelihood of success, one should set realistic goals and work persistently towards them. This statement reveals a simple truth: ambition alone means little unless it is anchored to attainable targets and sustained effort. A realistic goal keeps us moving instead of despairing. If a beginner runner vows to finish a marathon next week, failure is almost certain, and disappointment soon kills motivation. However, by aiming first at three kilometres, then five, and finally the full distance, the runner sets goals within reach and steadily raises the bar. Each small victory fuels the next. Yet reasonable goals mean nothing without persistence. My cousin, who dreamed of passing CET-6, did not expect overnight fluency. She fixed a modest daily plan of thirty new words and one reading passage, and she stuck to it for months. As a result, she cleared the exam comfortably. In this way, pairing sensible targets with steady work transforms a distant dream into a series of achievable steps. That is the surest road to success.

text: With the increasing application of AI technology, there is a growing concern that it may negatively impact human creativity. In my view, this worry is well-grounded, for excessive reliance on AI can gradually dull our capacity to think and create independently. The reason is straightforward. Creativity is a muscle that strengthens only through active practice. When we ask AI to generate essays, ideas, or solutions at the click of a button, we skip the very struggle that sparks original thinking. Take my own experience as an example. Last semester, I turned to an AI tool whenever an assignment felt difficult. Although the drafts came quickly, I soon realized that my mind had grown lazy: I could no longer brainstorm freely, and my writing lost its personal voice. Therefore, the concern deserves our serious attention. AI should serve as a helpful assistant rather than a replacement for our own minds. Only by keeping our thinking active can we ensure that technology enriches, rather than erodes, human creativity.

text: In an era of rapid social development, it is vitally important to enhance young people's sense of responsibility. As society changes at an unprecedented pace, young people often face distractions and pressures that weaken their commitment to family, community, and the future. Without a strong sense of responsibility, they may become self-centered and short-sighted. The decline of responsibility among youth is partly caused by the instant gratification culture brought by technology and social media. Many young people are used to receiving immediate rewards and may avoid duties that require long-term effort. To address this problem, schools and families should work together to cultivate accountability through real tasks and role models. For example, involving students in community service can help them understand the value of contributing to society. In conclusion, enhancing young people's sense of responsibility is not only a personal virtue but also a social necessity. Only when the younger generation takes responsibility seriously can society achieve sustainable development and harmony.

text: Faced with growing globalization,students realize that a deep understanding of traditional Chinese culture helps cultivate cultural confidence. In an age when Western brands, movies and festivals flood daily life, many young people begin to look back at their own roots. They find that cultural confidence cannot be borrowed from outside; it must grow from real knowledge of what their ancestors created. The reason is not hard to understand. Globalization exposes us to different values, yet it also makes us question who we are. Only by learning the ideas behind Confucianism, the beauty of calligraphy, or the spirit of traditional festivals can we answer that question with pride. Take the Spring Festival as an example: those who understand its meaning of reunion and renewal celebrate it not out of habit, but out of identity. Therefore, college students should actively read classics, visit museums and practice folk arts. The deeper we understand traditional Chinese culture, the more confident we become in facing the world.

text: Pasting Spring Festival couplets is an important custom for Chinese people during the Spring Festival. A Spring Festival couplet consists of a pair of poetic lines and a four-character horizontal scroll. Both the lines and the scroll are written in gold or black on red paper, with red symbolizing good luck and gold symbolizing wealth. The couplets are pasted on both sides of the door and above the doorframe. The poetic lines reflect the features of traditional Chinese poetry: the two lines have the same number of characters and are related in content. While the horizontal scroll highlights the theme of the couplet, it also adds the finishing touch. With concise words, Spring Festival couplets depict vivid images and express good wishes. Finally, when every household pastes Spring Festival couplets, people realize that the Spring Festival has officially begun.
